questions.q: Per this lesson, what does a real data retention policy cover, beyond just "when do we delete this"?
options: Only the deletion date, nothing else
The record's full lifecycle: how long it stays actively usable, whether and when it's archived, and only then when it's finally deleted
Only which users are allowed to see the record
Only whether the record was created through the UI or the API
questions.explain: The lesson frames retention as a lifecycle policy spanning active use, archiving, and eventual deletion -- not a single deletion decision.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say Field History Tracking and Field Audit Trail are NOT themselves a record retention policy, even though both involve configurable retention periods?
options: Because they don't actually retain any data at all
Because they answer "what changed on this record and when," not "how long should the record itself continue to exist" -- that's a separate decision
Because they are identical features with no real difference
Because only custom objects can use either feature
questions.explain: Both features track change history (useful for audit/traceability), but neither decides how long the record as a whole should exist -- that's the distinct question a retention policy has to answer.

questions.q: What misconception about "archived" data does this lesson correct?
options: That archived data can ever be restored
That once data is archived, it stops occupying storage or no longer needs to be accounted for -- archiving changes where/how data is accessed, not whether it still exists or still costs something
That archiving is only available to Salesforce Shield customers
That archived data is immediately and permanently deleted
questions.explain: The lesson states directly that archived field history (and Salesforce-native archiving generally) still occupies storage -- true low-cost long-term retention usually means exporting outside the platform.

questions.q: What caution does this lesson give about using Salesforce's native Mass Delete tool against production data?
options: Mass Delete cannot be undone in any way, so it should never be used
Before running it, export/report on the records first, and account for child records that cascade-delete with the parent (e.g., a Case's related Emails and Comments)
Mass Delete only works on custom objects, never standard ones
Mass Delete automatically respects every retention policy without configuration
questions.explain: The lesson recommends exporting/reporting first and being aware of cascading child-record deletion as practical safeguards before running a bulk deletion tool.

questions.q: According to this lesson, how should a retention policy typically reconcile a multi-year regulatory retention requirement with an individual's data-erasure request that touches the same records?
options: Always honor the erasure request and delete the entire record, regardless of the legal retention requirement
Always ignore the erasure request since legal retention requirements override everything
Anonymize the specific fields that identify the individual while retaining the aggregate or legally-required record shell, planned for in advance rather than improvised under pressure
Permanently lock the records so neither requirement can ever be acted on
questions.explain: The lesson describes anonymizing identifying fields while keeping the legally-required record shell as the usual resolution, and stresses this needs to be planned for in the policy itself, not improvised when a request actually arrives.
